# About TK Partners Certified Public Accountant

## Identity

TK Partners Certified Public Accountant is a regional CPA firm. Its tagline is "Expert Accounting Services for Your Business." The firm provides outsourced accounting, tax, and estate and trust services to individuals and businesses, including small businesses, wineries, agricultural operations, restaurants, and estates and trusts.

**Locations and contact**
- Walla Walla Office: 5 W. Alder, Suite 215, Walla Walla, WA 99362
- Moses Lake Office: 1000 South Pioneer Way, Moses Lake, WA 98837
- Phone: 509 529-0941
- Email: info@tkpartners.com
- Website: https://tkpartners.com
- Primary call to action: Contact us

**Geographic scope:** Regional, serving Eastern Washington and the surrounding area from the two offices above.

**Team:** The firm is led by Kristal Hassler, CPA (CEO & Partner) and Mike Lemm, CPA (Principal). Client Managers include Carrie Shelton, Ellen Camp, Cameron Lewis, Erin Denney, and Connor McCaw (all CPAs), plus Missy Collin. Anne Riney is Director of Operations. Kristine Huntsman is Firm Administrator, and Linnea Nygren is Client Experience Ambassador. A group of Client Accounting Specialists supports day-to-day client work. The firm describes its team as CPAs and client accounting specialists who coach clients with patience and empathy and work to improve every day.

**Core services**
- **Outsourced Accounting:** Virtual bookkeeper, payroll, and tax. It gives growing businesses timely, relevant financial information to support confident decisions.
- **Business & Personal Income Tax:** Tax preparation, tax planning, and year-round tax advice. Delivery is through a secure, paperless process with digital document upload and e-signing.
- **Estates & Trusts:** Estate and trust planning, business continuity planning, asset protection, estate tax mitigation, and fiduciary administration. The work is coordinated with clients' attorneys, financial managers, and bankers.
- **Business Foundation Services:** Entity type analysis and accounting system setup for new businesses.

**Values:** The firm's five core values are Excellence, Leadership, Drive, Friendship, and Flexibility. Its values statement describes leading with empathy and kindness, treating clients with the patience and guidance of a compassionate coach, working to alleviate clients' pain points, improving daily, valuing relationships with clients and each other, and adapting to clients' changing needs.

**Voice:** Warm, supportive, and professional, with a partnership-oriented tone, light wordplay, and plain-language explanations. The aspiration is a caring, encouraging coach who is still highly competent: approachable but expert, never stiff or salesy. Example: "We're not just here to file your numbers. We're in your corner all year long, translating the tax jargon and helping you make your next move with confidence."

## Positioning & Differentiation

**Positioning statement:** A supportive partner, not just an accountant, with industry specialization in wineries, agriculture, and restaurants.

**Who the firm serves:** Small business owners, winery owners, farmers, ranchers and agricultural businesses, restaurant owners, startups and established companies, trustees and estate administrators, and individuals and families needing tax and estate planning.

**What clients need:** Reliable bookkeeping and payroll without billing surprises, proactive year-round tax and planning advice, industry-specific accounting (wine, agriculture, restaurants), and plain-language guidance through estates and trusts.

**Differentiators**
- A supportive, caring partner approach rather than a once-a-year transactional relationship.
- A fixed monthly fee for bookkeeping, with no billing surprises.
- A secure digital tax process with document upload and e-signing.
- Year-round advisory support, including tax planning, rather than filing only at tax time.
- Industry-specific accounting for wineries, agriculture, and restaurants.
- Plain-language explanations of tax and financial jargon.
- Estate and trust expertise, shown in dedicated service pages and in-depth articles on topics such as basis tracking, gift tax safe harbor, living trust myths, and inheritance costs.

## Industries Served

### Wineries
Specialized outsourced accounting for winery owners, including inventory management, cost accounting, and alcohol regulation compliance.

- **Value proposition:** Accountants who understand winery inventory, cost accounting, and alcohol regulations, so owners can focus on the wine.
- **Pain points:** Tracking inventory and cost of goods across vintages; alcohol regulatory compliance and reporting; bookkeeping that doesn't fit seasonal cash flow.
- **Focus areas:** Alcohol regulation compliance; inventory management and cost accounting.
- **Typical triggers:** A compliance issue or audit scare, or growth (a new tasting room, more distribution) that outgrows the current bookkeeper.

### Agriculture
Outsourced accounting for farmers, ranchers, and agricultural businesses, including farm budgets, subsidies, grants, and asset depreciation.

- **Value proposition:** Outsourced accounting built around ag realities, covering budgets, grants, and depreciation, with year-round planning instead of a once-a-year tax filing.
- **Pain points:** Farm budgeting and unpredictable income; tracking subsidies and grants; asset depreciation and tax planning.
- **Focus areas:** Farm budgets; subsidies and grants; asset depreciation; farm tax planning.
- **Typical triggers:** A large equipment purchase, land or operation expansion, or a tax surprise at year-end.

### Restaurants
Outsourced accounting for restaurants, covering inventory, cost accounting, payroll, tax filings, and food service regulatory compliance.

- **Value proposition:** A fixed monthly fee for bookkeeping, payroll, and tax, so owners get accurate numbers without billing surprises.
- **Pain points:** Thin margins and food cost control; payroll and tip complexity; inventory tracking; food service regulatory and tax compliance.
- **Focus areas:** Inventory and cost accounting; payroll and tax filings; food service regulatory compliance.
- **Typical triggers:** Opening a new location or restaurant, falling behind on books or payroll, or unclear profitability.

### Businesses
Outsourced accounting for startups and established companies, including financial planning, tax compliance, and cost management.

- **Value proposition:** A supportive partner for setup, bookkeeping, tax, and planning year-round, not just at filing time.
- **Pain points:** No financial system or entity structure in place; tax compliance; cost management; no time for the books.
- **Focus areas:** Financial planning, tax compliance, and cost management; entity type analysis and accounting system setup through Business Foundation Services.
- **Typical triggers:** Starting a business, outgrowing spreadsheets, or needing an entity-type decision or financial planning.

### Estates & Trusts
Tax administration and accounting support for trustees and estate administrators.

- **Value proposition:** Patient, plain-language guidance through estate and trust tax administration, so trustees can fulfill their duties with confidence.
- **Pain points:** Unfamiliar fiduciary tax rules; basis tracking and gift tax questions; the administrative burden on trustees during a stressful time.
- **Typical triggers:** A death or trust funding that makes someone a trustee or administrator, or an estate plan that needs updating.

## Estate planning that starts with the tax picture

TK Partners is an estate planning CPA in Walla Walla that handles the tax and numbers side of your plan while your attorney handles the legal documents. We support estate and trust planning, business continuity, asset protection, estate tax mitigation, and fiduciary administration for individuals, families, and trustees across Eastern Washington.

If you are not sure where to start, you are in good company. Most families begin with one question, like "what happens to the farm?" or "do we need a trust?" We turn that into a plan you can follow. Here is what that includes:

- **Estate and trust planning:** the numbers behind your wishes, including support for revocable and irrevocable trust setup.
- **Business continuity planning:** keeping a family business running through a transition.
- **Asset protection:** structuring ownership so what you built stays protected.
- **Estate tax mitigation:** reducing what the IRS and Washington State can claim.
- **Fiduciary administration:** accounting and tax support for trustees and administrators.

Think of us as the part of your plan that keeps good intentions from turning into surprise bills.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## How can you protect and pass on what you have built?

Federal estate tax gets most of the headlines, but Washington has its own estate tax, and it starts at a much lower threshold. A family that owes nothing federally can still owe the state. Thresholds change, so we confirm the current numbers with you instead of quoting them from memory.

One point settles a common search: Washington has no inheritance tax. Beneficiaries do not pay a state tax simply for receiving an inheritance. They can still face income tax questions on things like retirement accounts or the sale of inherited property, which is why beneficiary tax planning matters.

Good estate tax planning usually comes down to four things:

- Estimating what your estate could owe at the federal and state level, then modeling ways to lower it.
- Choosing how assets are titled and held, which is the heart of asset protection.
- Tracking basis, the starting value used to calculate taxable gain, so heirs are not overtaxed later.
- Looking past the next generation, since multi-generational wealth planning means thinking about grandchildren, not just children.

Plans also go stale. A marriage, a divorce, a new grandchild, a death in the family, or the sale of a business can all change the math. If your plan was written before one of those, it is worth a second look.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: vineyard-family-succession-planning.jpg | alt: "Family owners walking through a vineyard row discussing the future of their winery" | query: "vineyard owners walking rows" -->
## Wineries, farms, and family businesses that need a succession plan

For a winery or a farm, the estate is rarely cash. It is land, equipment, barrels, and vintages sitting in inventory. When an owner passes away without a plan, heirs can be forced to sell part of the operation just to cover the tax bill. That is a hard way to learn what the estate was worth.

We work with winery owners and farm and ranch families across Eastern Washington on winery estate planning and agricultural estate planning. Business continuity planning and business succession planning are part of the same conversation: who runs it, who owns it, and how the tax works when the keys change hands.

The moments that usually start the conversation:

- A large equipment or land purchase.
- An expansion, like a new tasting room or more acres.
- An owner who is getting older and has not yet named a successor.

Erin Denney, CPA, our Tax Manager, brings entity structuring and multi-year tax strategy to closely-held and family-run businesses. Her work helps owner-operators choose how the business is held today, so the transfer tomorrow costs less. Already working with us on your books? We can pull your winery or ag numbers into the plan from day one. See how we support [wineries](/wineries) and [agriculture](/agriculture).

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image-left | image: trustee-reviewing-estate-paperwork.jpg | alt: "Trustee sitting at a desk reviewing estate paperwork with a calculator and laptop" | query: "person reviewing estate paperwork desk" -->
## What do you do when you suddenly become a trustee or administrator?

One phone call, one funeral, or one signed trust, and suddenly you are the trustee. Nobody hands you a manual. You are now a fiduciary, which simply means you are legally responsible for managing someone else's assets with care. Fiduciary tax rules are unfamiliar, basis tracking is confusing, gift tax questions pop up, and it all lands during a difficult season.

We take the accounting and tax weight off your shoulders and explain each step in plain language. If a term needs defining, we define it. Here is what we handle for trust administration in Walla Walla, WA and across Eastern Washington:

- **Fiduciary accounting:** recording what comes in, what goes out, and what you owe beneficiaries.
- **Trust accounting:** clean, ongoing records for trusts that continue after a death.
- **Probate accounting:** the financial reports that go with the court process.
- **Estate settlement:** paying final bills and taxes, then closing things out properly.
- **Trust and estate tax return preparation:** including the fiduciary income tax return and any estate tax filings.

You do not have to figure this out alone. For a deeper look at the tax side, visit our [estate and trust tax administration](/estate-trust-tax-administration) page.

Families and trustees do not always live down the road. Our secure, paperless process lets you upload documents and e-sign from wherever you are, so a trustee in another state can stay fully involved. Estate work is scoped to your situation, and we talk through fees before we start.

### An initial conversation
We listen first. You tell us what is in the estate, what worries you, and what your attorney has already done.

### Coordination with your attorney
With your permission, we work directly with your estate attorney, so the legal documents and the tax plan fit together.

### Ongoing tax and accounting support
We keep the records, track basis, and prepare the returns, whether you need family trust administration in Washington or a one-time estate settlement.

### Year-round check-ins
We do not disappear after filing. Regular check-ins catch life changes and tax law shifts before they become problems.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: winery-barrel-room-tax.jpg | alt: "Oak wine barrels stacked in a winery cellar with a glass of red wine" | query: "winery barrel room" -->
## Winery tax planning that follows your vintages

Wine is not a one-year product, and your books shouldn't treat it like one. Inventory and cost of goods move across vintages, and a bookkeeper who doesn't track them leaves your tax return resting on guesses. Alcohol regulatory compliance and reporting add another layer, and the numbers you report there need to agree with the numbers on your return.

Owners often start looking for new help after a compliance issue or an audit scare. Others call when growth catches up with them: a new tasting room, wider distribution, a bookkeeper who has reached the edge of what they know. Both are good moments to start.

Winery tax planning in Walla Walla works best with accountants who understand winery inventory, cost accounting and alcohol regulations. That is the whole point of working with us. You focus on the wine, and we keep the [winery books](/wineries) and the return in step with each other.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: farm-field-equipment.jpg | alt: "Tractor working a wheat field at sunset in farmland" | query: "farmer tractor wheat field" -->
## How can farm and ranch tax preparation avoid a year-end surprise?

The worst tax news arrives in December or January, when nothing can be done about it. Farm income is unpredictable, so a strong year and a tax bill you didn't see coming often show up together.

Planning during the year changes that. We look at where income is running, then decide what to do about it while there is still time to act. That includes how subsidies and grants are tracked and reported, so they land in the right place on your return.

Depreciation is the other big lever. A large equipment purchase, new land, or an expansion of the operation all change your tax picture. Talk to us before you sign, and we can plan the depreciation around the purchase instead of reacting to it afterward.

If you need agricultural tax preparation or farm tax services in Walla Walla, our [agriculture team](/agriculture) builds the plan around ag realities: budgets, grants, depreciation and a calendar that follows the seasons.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: restaurant-owner-ledger.jpg | alt: "Restaurant owner reviewing paperwork at a table inside a busy dining room" | query: "restaurant owner reviewing paperwork" -->
## Restaurant tax services for thin margins and tip-heavy payroll

Restaurants run on thin margins, so a small error in food cost or payroll shows up fast. Tips make payroll more complicated, inventory is always moving, and food service tax compliance has its own rules. If your books are behind, your tax return inherits every gap.

Restaurant owners often reach out at a turning point. They are opening a new location, falling behind on books or payroll, or unsure whether the place is actually making money.

Our answer is a fixed monthly fee for bookkeeping, payroll and tax. Your return is built from books that stay current all year, and your bill never surprises you. Restaurant tax services in Walla Walla should give you accurate numbers you can use on a Tuesday, not just a form you file in the spring. See how we work with [restaurant owners](/restaurants).

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## How does year-round tax planning in Walla Walla work beyond filing season?

Tax questions don't keep a filing calendar, so ask yours whenever it comes up. Call us in the summer before a big purchase. Call us in the fall when a good year makes you nervous. Year-round advisory support is part of how TK Partners works, because the best tax decisions are made before the deadline.

Erin Denney, CPA, is our Tax Manager, and multi-year tax strategy for owner-operators is a focus of her work. Owners of closely held wineries, farms and restaurants often face the same questions: how the business should be structured, when to time income and expenses, and what a decision this year means for the next three. Erin helps owners map those answers out across several years instead of one return at a time.

Before a big purchase or an expansion, we review entity structure and timing together. That is CPA tax planning in Walla Walla built around your plans. It gives you tailored tax strategies that fit your operation, with professional tax planning for the owner and preparation for the whole household.

### Business foundation services
URL: /what-we-do/business-foundation-services

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## Start with the structure your operation will grow into

A winery adds a tasting room and starts shipping through distributors. A rancher signs for another parcel and a piece of equipment that needs its own payment plan. A restaurateur opens a second location across town. Each owner is making a big move, and each move asks the same quiet question: is the business built to hold what comes next?

Business foundation services in Walla Walla at TK Partners answer it with two things: an entity type analysis and an accounting system setup. Our CPAs in the Walla Walla and Moses Lake offices sit down with you before anything is signed, explain the choices in plain language, and build a structure that fits how you earn money. You get a coach in your corner, not a form-filler. Think of it as pouring the concrete before you frame the house.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: entity-type-analysis-meeting.jpg | alt: "CPA explaining business structure options to two owners at a conference table" | query: "accountant explaining options to business owners" -->
## Choosing between an LLC, S corporation and C corporation

The right answer depends on your operation, which is why our entity type analysis starts with your numbers. We weigh four things: your tax exposure, how you will pay yourself as an owner, your personal liability, and what happens at a future sale or succession. Whether you are weighing an S-corp vs LLC question or looking at LLC formation in Walla Walla, the goal is the same: a business entity selection you will still be glad of in five years.

- **Winery:** Several owners, an alcohol license and inventory held in barrels and bottles across vintages. How profits are split and how the license is held both shape which entity fits.
- **Agriculture:** Family ownership, land and equipment depreciation. Structure decides how those assets are held and how they pass to the next generation.
- **Restaurant:** Owner pay, payroll and tip complexity. The entity you choose changes how you draw income and how payroll is set up.

A wrong choice is expensive to unwind, and it usually surfaces at the worst time, like a sale or a tax bill. Erin Denney, CPA, our Tax Manager, builds this work around entity structuring and multi-year tax strategy for owner-operators, so today's decision still makes sense in year five.

We advise on structure and tax impact. State filing and legal drafting steps are coordinated with your attorney.

<!-- block: feature-grid | variant: 3-col -->
## Books built around how your industry earns its money

An accounting system set up for a generic business will strain the first time a harvest comes in or a tip pool gets split. We build the chart of accounts and reporting around your industry from day one, so the first year-end holds no surprises.

### Winery business setup in Walla Walla
icon: ClipboardCheck

Inventory and cost of goods tracked across vintages, so you know what each bottle costs to make. Reporting is set up for alcohol regulatory compliance, which keeps an audit scare from becoming a scramble.

### Agriculture business formation in Walla Walla
icon: TrendingUp

Farm budgeting that makes room for unpredictable income. Grants and subsidies are tracked as they arrive, and asset depreciation is organized before the equipment invoice lands.

### Restaurant accounting setup in Walla Walla
icon: Receipt

Food cost and thin margins visible every month, not at year-end. Tips and payroll are configured correctly from the first shift, and inventory tracking is built into the system.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: fixed-monthly-fee-bookkeeping.jpg | alt: "Restaurant owner reviewing monthly bookkeeping reports on a laptop with an accountant" | query: "restaurant owner reviewing finances laptop" -->

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: tax-documents-checklist.jpg | alt: "Tax forms and a checklist laid out on a desk beside a laptop" | query: "tax paperwork checklist desk laptop" -->
## Tax documents to gather for your personal and business return

Gather these before we sit down together and your return moves faster. The right paperwork also makes year-round tax advice possible: we can spot a planning move in March instead of finding it in April. This list supports our [Business & Personal Income Tax](/what-we-do/income-tax) service, and a printable PDF version of this tax documentation checklist is available from our team on request.

- Personal income tax forms: W-2s from every employer, 1099s for interest, dividends, retirement and freelance income, and 1098s for mortgage interest or tuition
- Last year's filed return, so we can match carryovers and spot changes
- Business tax forms and records: a current profit and loss statement and balance sheet
- Payroll reports, including quarterly filings
- Asset purchase records with the date, cost and invoice
- **Form W-9** (Request for Taxpayer Identification Number and Certification): the form a contractor or vendor supplies so you can issue a 1099
- **Form 8821** (Tax Information Authorization): lets us view your IRS records without speaking for you
- **Form 2848** (Power of Attorney and Declaration of Representative): lets us represent you before the IRS, such as answering a notice

### Track your tax refund status
URL: /resources/refund-tracker

<!-- block: process-steps | variant: vertical -->
## Check your federal refund status in three steps

Waiting on a refund tests everyone's patience, but you can at least swap "any day now" for an actual status. If you're asking where is my tax refund Walla Walla WA, the answer almost always lives on one IRS page. Washington has no state personal income tax, so the refund you're tracking is almost always federal.

### Gather three details
You need your Social Security number or ITIN, your filing status, and the exact refund amount on your return, in whole dollars. Keep your return open beside you.

### Enter them in the IRS tool
Open the [IRS Where's My Refund? tool](https://www.irs.gov/wheres-my-refund), the official way to check your federal tax refund status online. It works about 24 hours after you e-file, or about four weeks after you mail a paper return. Pick the tax year you filed, then enter your details.

### Read your status message
"Return Received" means the IRS has your return. "Refund Approved" means your amount is confirmed and a send date is being set. "Refund Sent" means it's on its way. For direct deposit, your bank may need a few extra days to post it. The tool updates once a day, usually overnight, so checking every hour won't change the answer.

<!-- block: content-table -->
## How long a tax refund takes to arrive

The IRS issues most e-filed refunds in under 21 days. Paper returns take longer, and direct deposit beats a mailed check because there's no mail time. Here is the estimated tax refund timeline by filing method:

| How you filed | How you get paid | Typical timing |
|---|---|---|
| E-filed | Direct deposit | Most refunds in under 21 days |
| E-filed | Mailed check | Same processing, plus mail time |
| Paper return | Direct deposit | Four weeks or longer |
| Paper return | Mailed check | Four weeks or longer, plus mail time |

A return flagged for review or correction can take longer than any of these.

**Amended returns run on their own clock.** They don't appear in the regular tool. Use the IRS [Where's My Amended Return?](https://www.irs.gov/filing/wheres-my-amended-return-1) tool, which usually shows a status about three weeks after you file Form 1040-X. Amended returns are reviewed by hand, and current IRS guidance says to allow up to 16 weeks.

The fastest route to a clean submission is a complete, e-filed return. Sending your documents through our secure digital upload and e-signing process helps get it there without missing pieces.

*This guidance applies to tax year 2024 returns, filed in 2025, so use it when you're checking 2024 tax refund status. Last reviewed: [insert date of final IRS check].*

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: tax-refund-paperwork-review.jpg | alt: "CPA and client reviewing a delayed tax refund notice together at a desk" | query: "accountant helping client tax paperwork" -->
## What to do when your refund is late or missing

A late refund is stressful, but it's rarely a verdict on your return. Most delays trace back to one of a few causes, and each has a next step. If you need Walla Walla CPA tax refund help, we deal with the IRS alongside you, with your authorization.

- **Identity verification hold.** The IRS mails a letter before releasing the refund. Follow the letter's instructions exactly. If you've responded and weeks pass with no movement, call us.
- **Math errors or an e-file rejection.** A rejected e-file never reaches "Return Received," so fix the error and resend. A math correction usually brings a notice and a delay. Send us the notice and we'll read it with you.
- **Direct deposit details that don't match.** If the bank rejects the deposit, the IRS typically mails a paper check instead. Confirm your account and routing numbers, and call us if the check hasn't arrived.
- **An offset against another debt.** Past-due federal or state debts can absorb part or all of a refund. You'll get a notice explaining where the money went. Bring it to us if the numbers don't add up.

IRS guidance says to call when it's been more than 21 days since you e-filed, more than six weeks since you mailed a paper return, or the tool tells you to. Call us first if you'd rather not wait on hold. A missing tax refund in Walla Walla is solvable, and you don't have to solve it alone.

<!-- block: industry-cards | variant: 3-col -->
## Refunds for wineries, farms, and restaurants

A business refund can run on a different timeline from a personal one. If you file as an owner-operator on a Form 1040, the Where's My Refund? tool tracks it like any individual return. Entity returns are different: the IRS tool doesn't cover them, so we pull IRS transcripts or call the IRS with you to see where things stand. We can't promise amounts or dates, but we can tell you exactly where yours is.

### Wineries
icon: ClipboardCheck

Winery refunds often trace back to inventory and cost-of-goods timing across vintages. When costs land in a different year than expected, estimates can overshoot. We reconcile that before filing, then help with winery tax refund tracking afterward.

### Agriculture
icon: Wrench

A large equipment purchase plus depreciation can leave a farm with overpaid estimates. Farm tax refund questions in Walla Walla usually start here. Where the refund or credit shows up depends on how the return was filed.

### Restaurants
icon: Receipt

Overpaid estimates and payroll timing, like quarter-end deposits and tip reporting, can create an overpayment. The return decides whether it's refunded or applied to next year's estimates. For any restaurant business tax refund, we check which one happened.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: year-round-tax-planning.jpg | alt: "Accountant and winery owner reviewing tax planning documents together at a desk" | query: "accountant client reviewing tax planning" -->
## Plan ahead so next year's refund holds no surprises

A big refund isn't a prize, and a surprise bill isn't bad luck. Both usually mean withholding or estimated payments were off all year. For farm and winery owners, the surprise tends to land at year-end, after the equipment purchase or the big harvest is already done. For restaurant owners, unclear profitability turns estimates into guesses.

We adjust through the year instead of only at filing time. That works because the books stay current: our fixed monthly fee for bookkeeping means no billing surprises, and the numbers are fresh enough to plan from. Erin Denney, CPA, our Tax Manager, builds multi-year tax strategy for owner-operators, including entity structuring. Learn more about our [income tax services](/what-we-do/income-tax).

## How TK Partners protects your information

This policy covers two groups: visitors to the TK Partners website, and clients of our Walla Walla and Moses Lake, WA offices. If you knew us as TKCPA, you're in the right place. Same firm, new name.

This is the TK Partners accounting privacy policy, and we wrote it in plain language, not legalese. You trust us with bank records, payroll files and tax documents. You should be able to read what happens to them without hiring a lawyer to translate. No surprises in your bill, and none in how your information is handled.

Effective date: [EFFECTIVE DATE: LEGAL REVIEWER TO FILL IN]

Last updated: [LAST UPDATED DATE: LEGAL REVIEWER TO FILL IN]

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## What information we collect

We collect two kinds of information, and the first is much bigger than the second.

### What clients share for accounting, payroll and tax work

To do the work well, we need real records. Depending on what you hire us for, that can include:

- Identity details, such as your name, address, date of birth, Social Security number or EIN
- Bank statements, credit card activity, payroll records and prior tax returns
- Tax documents such as W-2s, 1099s and K-1s

The specifics depend on your business. [Winery](/wineries) clients send inventory and cost records across vintages. [Farm and ranch](/agriculture) clients send budgets and grant or subsidy paperwork, so agricultural accounting privacy matters from the first upload. [Restaurant](/restaurants) owners send payroll and tip records. Whatever your industry, this is sensitive material, and we treat it that way.

### What the website collects

When you use our site, we may receive:

- Contact form entries, including your name, email address, phone number and message
- Emails you send us directly
- Standard analytics and cookie data, such as pages visited, browser type and approximate location [CONFIRM WITH FIRM: analytics tools in use]

Client information security in accounting starts with collecting only what the job needs. We don't ask for more.

## Resources

### Do the math behind renting vs. buying a home
URL: /resources/do-the-math-behind-renting-vs-buying-a-home

A winery owner in Walla Walla who asks "should I buy or keep renting?" is usually asking three questions at once. What will the monthly cost be? What happens to the cash I need for harvest? And will a lender count my income the way I do? Most buy-versus-rent articles answer only the first, and they answer it with a mood ("rent is throwing money away") or a market guess ("prices might drop"). Neither belongs in a financial decision.

This post treats the choice the way a CPA treats any big move: as a change to your personal financial statement. Put the numbers on the page, then decide.

## Start with your balance sheet, not the listing

Before you compare a mortgage payment to a rent check, write down what you own and owe today. Cash, brokerage and retirement accounts, your ownership stake in the winery, vehicles, and any debt, personal or business, that you have guaranteed.

The [Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances](https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/files/scf20.pdf) shows that a primary residence is the largest asset on many American households' balance sheets. For a winery owner, that has a catch. Your balance sheet is probably already lopsided. Barrels, tanks, vineyard improvements, and inventory aging in the cellar are all tied up in one business. A house adds a second large asset you cannot sell quickly.

So the first question is about liquidity. After you buy, how many months of personal expenses and business obligations could you cover without selling anything? If the honest answer is "fewer than six," the purchase may be sound but the timing needs work. If you are also weighing other big purchases, our look at [leasing versus buying a vehicle](/resources/auto-leasing-vs-buying-which-makes-more-sense) uses the same cash-flow-first approach.

## Price the true monthly cost of owning

The mortgage payment is the number everyone quotes and the least complete one. A fair comparison counts five things:

- **Interest.** The cost of borrowing. Principal is not a cost, because it builds equity, so leave it out of the comparison.
- **Property tax.** Budget roughly 1% of assessed value as a starting assumption, then check the actual rate for the parcel.
- **Insurance.** Homeowner's coverage, plus any rider if part of the property is used for the business.
- **Maintenance.** A common planning figure is 1% of the home's value per year. Older homes and rural well-and-septic properties often run higher.
- **Lost return on the down payment.** Cash you put into a house stops earning anything elsewhere. Count it.

That last item is the one people skip, and it often decides the answer.

## Run the comparison with real numbers

Here is an illustrative example. The inputs are assumptions, not a quote on any specific property, so swap in your own.

Suppose you are looking at a $550,000 home with 20% down ($110,000), a $440,000 loan at 6.75% over 30 years, and comparable rent of $2,300 a month.

| Monthly cost | Buying | Renting |
|---|---|---|
| Mortgage interest (year-one average) | $2,450 | n/a |
| Property tax (1% of value) | $458 | n/a |
| Insurance | $150 | $20 |
| Maintenance (1% of value) | $458 | n/a |
| Lost return on $110,000 at 5% | $458 | n/a |
| Rent | n/a | $2,300 |
| **Total economic cost** | **$3,974** | **$2,320** |

The actual mortgage payment is about $2,854, and roughly $4,850 of the first year's payments goes to principal. That is real savings, but it is savings you can only reach by selling or refinancing.

The gap is about $1,654 a month, or $19,850 a year. Divide that by the home's price and you get 3.6%. In year one, the home has to appreciate about 3.6% just for buying to match renting. Add roughly 6% in selling costs ($33,000) spread over a five-year hold, and the required appreciation climbs closer to 5% a year.

That does not mean buying is wrong. Rents rise, a fixed-rate loan does not, and over ten or fifteen years the math often tilts toward owning. But the timeline matters more than the market forecast. If you may sell, move, or restructure the business within five years, the same house looks very different than it does over fifteen.

## What the mortgage interest deduction saves a winery owner

Many buyers assume the deduction makes owning much cheaper. Sometimes it does. Often it barely changes anything.

[IRS Topic No. 505](https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc505) explains that you can deduct home mortgage interest only if you itemize, and that the deduction applies to interest on up to $750,000 of acquisition debt for most recent loans. Washington has no state income tax, so the usual itemized building blocks are thinner than in many states: mortgage interest, a capped amount of property tax, and charitable gifts.

Using the example above, year-one interest is about $29,400 and property tax is about $5,500, for roughly $34,900 in deductions. A married couple's standard deduction is around $30,000. Itemizing only gets you about $4,900 above what you would deduct anyway. At a 24% bracket, that is roughly $1,200 of tax savings, or about $100 a month. Worth having, but it will not close a $1,654 monthly gap.

The picture can change if part of the property is genuinely used in the business, such as a tasting room, a vineyard block, or a dedicated office. Business-use portions are treated differently from personal ones, and the allocation needs to be documented before closing, not reconstructed in March. Our [tax preparation and planning team](/what-we-do/income-tax) sets this up with owners before they sign.

## Your down payment competes with your barrels

In most households, the down payment competes with a vacation fund or a car. In a winery, it competes with working capital.

Think about your calendar. Crush season brings labor, fruit, and fuel costs all at once. Bottling runs need glass, closures, and labels paid up front, long before the wine sells. A new barrel program or a tank purchase can easily outweigh a down payment on its own. If you move $110,000 out of cash in August, you may be borrowing against the business line of credit by October to cover what that cash would have handled.

That creates a quiet cost. You might pay 8% or 9% on the line of credit to protect a down payment that would have earned 5% elsewhere. In that case, the true price of the house is higher than the table shows.

A few ways owners handle it:

- **Smaller down payment with a larger reserve.** Putting 10% down raises the monthly cost, but it keeps $55,000 available for the cellar.
- **Timing the closing.** Closing in winter or early spring, after the cash from fall sales has landed, keeps the purchase out of the crush squeeze.
- **Separating the buckets.** Decide in advance which dollars are personal and which are business working capital, and do not let the house pull from the second bucket.

If your investment accounts are part of the down payment, review them first. Selling holdings in a taxable account can trigger capital gains, and it can throw off your target mix. Our piece on [balancing an investment portfolio for wineries](/resources/strategically-balancing-your-investment-portfolio-why-set-it) covers how to check that before you sell anything.

## Lenders read your tax return, so your tax strategy matters

Here is the tension that surprises owner-operators. A good tax strategy lowers your taxable income, and a mortgage underwriter qualifies you on, essentially, your taxable income.

Most lenders average two years of net income from your returns. Depreciation on equipment, bonus depreciation on a new press, and aggressive expense timing all shrink that figure. A winery that grew from $400,000 to $650,000 in revenue can still show modest owner income after good tax planning. Lenders may add back certain non-cash items, such as depreciation, but they can also discount income that is volatile or that comes from a pass-through entity's retained earnings.

If a home purchase is on your horizon within two years, that is worth planning for deliberately. The decision isn't "minimize tax" or "qualify for the loan." It is a multi-year question about which years you want to look strongest on paper. Erin Denney, CPA, our Tax Manager, works on this kind of multi-year strategy and entity structure with owner-operators, and the sequencing conversation is much easier eighteen months before an application than eighteen days before.

## A short worksheet to settle the question

You can do this on one page:

1. **List your current net worth and liquid cash.** Separate personal from business.
2. **Build the five-line ownership cost** with real quotes for insurance, the property's actual tax bill, and a maintenance figure you trust.
3. **Find the rent for a comparable home** and add 3% a year for growth.
4. **Calculate the break-even appreciation** the way the table above does, for a five-year and a ten-year hold.
5. **Stress-test your reserves.** Subtract the down payment and closing costs from your cash, then run a bad harvest or a slow tasting-room summer. Do you still have room?
6. **Check the tax side.** Will itemizing help, and how will your next two returns look to a lender?

If renting wins on the numbers, that is not a failure to build wealth. It may mean the cash is better used in the winery or in diversified investments, and you can revisit the question each year. If buying wins, you walk in knowing exactly why.

## Common Questions

**Is renting better than buying for a winery owner?**

It depends on your holding period and cash needs, not on a general rule. Renting often wins when you may move within five years or need the down payment for harvest costs and equipment. Buying tends to win over a ten-year-plus horizon with stable income and a healthy cash reserve.

**Does the mortgage interest deduction make buying worth it?**

Only if your itemized deductions exceed the standard deduction. In our example, interest plus property tax beat a roughly $30,000 standard deduction by about $4,900, worth around $1,200 a year at a 24% bracket. That helps, but it rarely decides the question alone.

**How much cash should I keep after a down payment?**

A common target is six months of combined personal and essential business expenses in accessible cash. Because wineries pay for fruit, labor, and bottling before revenue arrives, many owners aim higher than that before closing. We can model your seasonal low point so the number is based on your own calendar.

## Bring your numbers to someone in your corner

The right answer depends on your cash cycle, your tax picture, and how long you plan to stay. If you are weighing a purchase, [contact TK Partners](/contact) and we will build the rent-versus-buy comparison with you, using your actual winery cash flow and tax returns, so you can make the call with confidence.

### Take back control of subscription creep
URL: /resources/take-back-control-of-subscription-creep

Most winery owners can recite their biggest costs from memory: fruit, barrels, glass, labor, the tasting room lease. Ask about the 40th-largest cost and you get a shrug. That is where subscription creep lives. A reservation platform here, a second email tool there, a compliance add-on someone signed up for during one stressful harvest. None of them hurts on its own. Together they are a steady leak, and a leak gets fixed the same way any other budget line does: by measuring it, assigning it an owner, and reviewing it on a schedule.

## Why one $29 charge costs more than $29 a month

A $29 monthly charge feels too small to question. Run the numbers and it stops being small.

$29 a month is $348 a year. If your winery nets 15 percent after all expenses, you need about $2,320 in additional sales to pay for that one subscription, or roughly 52 bottles at $45. Nobody would approve a 52-bottle line item without asking what it buys. Yet that is exactly what an unreviewed subscription does.

Now multiply. Picture a hypothetical Walla Walla tasting room with 23 recurring charges averaging $48 a month. That is $1,104 a month, or $13,248 a year, and most owners would guess the number is under half that. If six of those subscriptions are unused or duplicated, cutting them frees $3,456 a year. That is a pallet of bottles, a season of tasting room hospitality training, or a meaningful piece of next year's barrel purchase.

The other problem is timing. Subscriptions rarely renew when cash is comfortable. Annual plans tend to hit in January or February, right after harvest bills and before release weekends bring tasting room traffic back. A $1,200 annual renewal you forgot about is a cash-flow event, not a rounding error.

## Where subscriptions hide in a winery

Wineries collect subscriptions faster than most businesses because the model has so many moving parts: production, tasting room, wine club, direct-to-consumer shipping, compliance. Each part brings its own software. Here is where we most often see charges pile up.

| Area | What tends to creep | What to check |
|---|---|---|
| Tasting room | Point-of-sale add-ons, reservation tools, music licensing | Are you paying monthly fees and per-transaction fees for the same function? |
| Wine club and DTC | Club management software, shipping and tax compliance tools, email and text platforms | Do two platforms overlap on customer data or messaging? |
| Cellar and production | Inventory apps, lab analysis tools, vineyard mapping | Does anyone still log in during the off-season? |
| Marketing | Design tools, stock photos, scheduling apps, extra seats | Are former interns and contractors still holding paid seats? |
| Office and admin | Cloud storage, video calls, password managers, phone lines | Are personal and business accounts mixed on one card? |
| Free trials | Trials that quietly converted to paid plans | Which charges started in the last 12 months, and who approved them? |

The most expensive subscriptions are rarely the biggest ones. They are the ones nobody owns. A tool bought by a former tasting room manager, still billing a card that now belongs to someone else, can run for two years before anyone asks about it.

## Run a 90-minute subscription audit

You do not need special software. You need your last 12 months of bank and credit card statements, a spreadsheet, and one uninterrupted block of time, ideally a slow Tuesday in the off-season rather than the week before crush.

**Step 1: Pull every recurring charge.** Go through 12 months, not 3. Annual and quarterly charges only show up when you look at a full year. Sort by vendor and flag anything that appears at regular intervals.

**Step 2: Build a simple register.** One row per subscription, with these columns: vendor, monthly cost, billing cycle (monthly, annual, usage-based), renewal date, who uses it, what it does, and last date it was used.

**Step 3: Assign an owner.** Every subscription gets one named person responsible for it. If nobody claims it, that is your first cancellation candidate.

**Step 4: Sort into three piles.** Keep (it earns its place), consolidate (two tools do one job), and cancel (unused or unclear). For the consolidate pile, ask whether your point-of-sale or club platform already includes the feature you are paying someone else to provide.

**Step 5: Check the contracts before you cancel.** Some annual plans renew automatically and cannot be refunded mid-term. Put the cancellation deadline on the calendar 30 days before renewal so you cancel on your terms.

**Step 6: Call the vendors that stay.** Ask about annual pricing, nonprofit or industry rates, or downgrading seats. A five-minute call sometimes trims a bill by 10 to 20 percent, and the worst answer is no.

Your credit card statements are the raw material here. If you are still deciding which card should carry recurring business charges, our piece on a [business credit card rewards strategy for Walla Walla wineries](/resources/business-credit-card-rewards-a-financial-strategy-for-busine) covers how to match cards to seasonal spending, so the audit and the card choice can work together.

## Make the leak visible in your books

An audit is a one-time fix. Your books are what keep the leak from reopening.

The usual culprit is a single catch-all account labeled "office expenses" or "miscellaneous." When a $14 charge and a $400 charge land in the same bucket as printer paper, nobody sees the total. A cleaner approach:

- Create a dedicated "Software and subscriptions" account, with sub-accounts by function: tasting room, wine club and DTC, production, marketing, admin.
- Code every recurring charge to the same sub-account every month, so trends show up in a report instead of in a surprise.
- Keep the winery's charges and the owner's personal streaming and app charges on separate cards. Personal subscriptions are not deductible, and mixing them in makes both the audit and your tax return harder to defend.

This is the kind of detail that gets lost when bookkeeping is squeezed between harvest tasks. It is also why we offer bookkeeping on a fixed monthly fee: the books get reviewed on schedule, and nobody is nervous about the meter running when they ask a question about a charge. If you want to see how that works for a winery, our [winery accounting services](/wineries) page walks through vintage-level cost accounting and compliance support alongside the monthly bookkeeping.

## Set a recurring expenses budget with a ceiling

Once the register exists, turn it into a budget. Treat recurring expenses the way you treat grape contracts: a known commitment that deserves a planned number.

A workable structure has three parts:

1. **A ceiling.** Pick a percentage of revenue for software and subscriptions and hold to it. Many owners find that setting the ceiling at last year's actual spend, minus the audit savings, is a realistic first target.
2. **A new-subscription rule.** Before anyone adds a tool, they name what it replaces or what revenue it supports. If it cannot be tied to one or the other, it waits a month.
3. **A quarterly 20-minute review.** Open the register, look at renewals in the next 90 days, and decide on each one. Put it on the calendar next to your quarterly estimated tax date so it actually happens.

Seasonality deserves its own line. A tasting room that runs full tilt in spring and fall can pause or downgrade some tools in slower months. Ask each vendor whether pausing is an option, and note it in the register. Cutting monthly expenses does not always mean canceling. Sometimes it means paying for the plan you need in January, not the one you needed in October.

The [AICPA-CIMA personal financial planning resources](https://www.aicpa-cima.com/resources/landing/personal-financial-planning) are a useful companion if you want to apply the same discipline to household recurring charges, which tend to creep right alongside the business ones.

## The tax side of the subscription list

Most software and subscriptions used to run the winery are ordinary business expenses, which means they reduce taxable income. That is a reason to track them well, not a reason to keep them. A deduction returns only a portion of what you spent, so a cancelled $29 subscription saves more cash than the deduction ever returned.

There are three places subscriptions create tax friction:

- **Mixed personal and business use.** A phone plan or cloud storage account used for both needs a reasonable allocation, and the allocation needs a basis you can explain.
- **Multi-year prepayments.** Paying three years upfront can complicate timing, so ask before you click.
- **Poor coding.** If subscriptions are scattered across five accounts, your preparer has to reconstruct them at tax time, which costs you time and invites missed deductions.

If you are not sure how your recurring charges fit into your year-end picture, our [tax preparation and planning](/what-we-do/income-tax) team can review them as part of year-round planning, rather than in April when it is too late to change anything.

## Common Questions

**How often should a winery audit its subscriptions?**

Do a full audit once a year, ideally in the off-season, and a 20-minute renewal review each quarter. The annual pass catches forgotten charges and duplicate tools. The quarterly check catches annual renewals before they hit your account, which matters most when cash is tight after harvest.

**What is a reasonable amount to spend on software and subscriptions?**

There is no universal percentage, because a winery with a large wine club and DTC shipping legitimately needs more software than a tasting-room-only operation. A better benchmark is your own prior year. Set the ceiling at last year's total minus audit savings, then watch the trend quarterly.

**Are business subscriptions tax deductible?**

Generally yes, when they are ordinary and necessary for running the winery. Personal subscriptions are not, and mixed-use accounts need a documented allocation. Deductions only return part of what you spend, so cancelling an unused subscription still saves more than keeping it for the write-off.

**Should I cancel a subscription I only use during crush or release season?**

Not necessarily. First ask the vendor about pausing or downgrading the plan in slow months. If neither option exists and the tool sits idle for more than four months, compare the cost of re-subscribing against a year of paying for downtime. Often cancelling and re-subscribing wins.

## Start with one honest look at the statements

Subscription creep is one of the easiest leaks to fix, because the money is already visible in your statements. It just needs someone to look. If you would like a second set of eyes, the TK Partners team in Walla Walla can walk through your recurring charges with you, set up your books so they stay visible, and fold the savings into your cash-flow plan for the year. [Reach out to us](/contact) and we will help you find the leak before it costs you another vintage's worth of margin.

### Business credit card rewards strategy for Walla Walla wineries
URL: /resources/business-credit-card-rewards-a-financial-strategy-for-busine

A winery runs on a strange mix of spending. There is the $40,000 barrel order in spring, the thousand small purchases at harvest, and the tasting room that somehow needs napkins every Tuesday. Put all of that on one random card and you collect a trickle of points. Match the card to the spending and you can turn the same dollars into real cash flow and a cleaner tax picture.

This post walks through how Walla Walla winery owners can build a business credit card rewards strategy on purpose, what the tax rules say about rewards, and how to keep points from turning your books into a puzzle.

## Map your spending by season before you pick a card

The best card for your winery depends on where your money goes and when. Pull twelve months of statements and sort them into categories. Then note the month each category spikes.

Here is an illustrative winery that spends about $216,000 a year on card-eligible expenses, apart from grape purchases:

| Category | Annual spend | Peak months |
|---|---|---|
| Bottles, corks, cartons, labels | $84,000 | Spring and summer bottling |
| Freight and wine club shipping | $30,000 | November and December |
| Advertising, events, and wine club marketing | $26,000 | Spring release, fall |
| Tasting room supplies and food | $22,000 | May through October |
| Software, POS, and subscriptions | $12,000 | Steady |
| Fuel, vehicle, and equipment parts | $14,000 | Harvest |
| Travel and trade shows | $10,000 | Winter and spring |
| Utilities and other | $18,000 | Steady |

The numbers are made up, but the pattern is common. Spending clusters around bottling, release season, and crush. A card that pays 2 percent on everything would earn this winery $4,320 a year. A card with a higher rate on shipping, advertising, or fuel might beat that, but only if those categories are big enough to matter. In this example they total $70,000, so a bonus category adds a few hundred dollars, not thousands.

Once you see your own table, the choice usually gets simpler. If one or two categories dominate, a category card may earn its keep. If your spending is scattered, a flat-rate card is easier to live with and easier to reconcile.

## Use the float to carry you through crush

Rewards get the attention, but the float is often worth more to a seasonal business. Depending on the card, a statement cycle plus a grace period can give you roughly 45 to 55 days between a purchase and the day cash leaves your bank account.

That matters in September and October. Harvest labor, fuel, lab work, and cleaning supplies all hit at once, while the revenue from last year's vintage trickles in through the tasting room and the wine club. Paying those costs by card and settling the full balance after the statement closes lets your cash work for you a few extra weeks.

The float only works if you pay in full. A $10,000 balance carried at 22 percent APR costs about $183 a month in interest. That wipes out a year of rewards on a $100,000 spending pace in roughly a month. Rewards are a discount for paying on time, not a reason to borrow.

## Know when a card is the wrong tool

Not every winery expense belongs on a card. Grape purchases are the big one. Growers often pay their own costs and prefer checks or ACH, and some vendors add a surcharge of 2.5 to 3 percent for card payments. If you pay $120,000 for fruit and a 3 percent surcharge applies, you spend $3,600 to earn maybe $2,400 in rewards. That is a loss with a points balance attached.

Before you move a large vendor to a card, ask three questions:

- Does the vendor charge a surcharge or raise the price for card payments?
- Does the card cap rewards in that category, or pay a lower rate on large single transactions?
- Will the charge strain your credit limit during a month when you need room for harvest costs?

Excise taxes and many regulatory payments follow their own payment rules and often come out of the bank account. Check the payment options before you plan around a card for them.

## Are credit card rewards taxable for businesses?

In most cases, no. The IRS has generally treated cash back and points earned from spending as a rebate on the purchase, not as income. You bought something, and the card issuer effectively gave you a discount.

There are exceptions worth knowing:

- **Bonuses with no purchase required.** A sign-up bonus for opening an account or making a deposit, with no spending attached, can be taxable income, and the issuer may send a Form 1099.
- **Referral payments.** Cash you receive for referring others is usually income.
- **Rewards from personal spending.** These are generally treated as a rebate, but mixing personal and business purchases creates a bigger problem than the rewards themselves.

The rebate treatment has a quiet implication. Strictly speaking, a rebate reduces the cost of what you bought. For a winery, that means rewards earned on bottling supplies are, in theory, a reduction of inventory cost. Rewards earned on advertising reduce an expense. The dollars involved are usually small, but the way you record them should be consistent and your CPA should sign off on it. The [IRS Small Business and Self-Employed Tax Center](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed) is a good starting point for the general rules, and your own situation deserves a conversation, not a guess.

Annual fees on a business card are generally deductible as a business expense. Interest on business purchases is generally deductible too, which is a poor reason to carry a balance, but it explains why the interest line shows up on your return.

## Keep rewards from muddying your books

A winery's books carry more weight than most. Inventory and cost of goods sold flow from what you spend across each vintage, and a card statement full of mixed purchases can bury that trail.

A few habits keep the picture clean:

1. **Code every card transaction to the right account.** Corks and glass belong in inventory or production costs. Tasting room napkins are an operating expense. A single "credit card" bucket hides the difference.
2. **Reconcile the card monthly, like a bank account.** The statement total should match what your books show, and any gap should be explained before the next cycle.
3. **Decide once how to record rewards.** Whether you book them as a reduction of expense or as other income when redeemed, pick a method and keep it steady. Switching every year makes your margins harder to compare.
4. **Issue employee cards with limits.** A tasting room manager and a cellar lead can each have a card with a spending cap and a category in mind. It beats reimbursing receipts weeks later.
5. **Keep personal charges off the business card.** Commingling is one of the fastest ways to turn a simple review into a long one, and it can cloud the line between owner draws and business expenses.

This is the part of the work our clients tend to hand off. With a fixed monthly fee for bookkeeping, you get this reconciliation done on a schedule, with no billing surprises when the statement is messy. Our [Insights library](/resources/category-insights-tk-partners-certified-public-accountant) covers other decisions like this one.

## Tie big purchases to your tax plan

Cards become more interesting when a large purchase is on the horizon, such as a new press, a forklift, a tasting room remodel, or a vehicle. Charging equipment can pull the deduction into the year you place it in service, and the rewards on a large purchase are real money. But a big charge also lifts your balance, your utilization, and the amount of cash you need on payment day.

Vehicle purchases deserve extra care. Our post on [leasing versus buying a car](/resources/auto-leasing-vs-buying-which-makes-more-sense) covers mileage, Section 179 limits, and how winery owners can weigh the cash-flow side before putting anything on plastic.

Erin Denney, CPA, our Tax Manager, works with closely-held owner-operators on entity structuring and multi-year tax strategy. Her view of a card strategy is that it sits inside a longer plan. If you expect a profitable year followed by an expansion year, the timing of large purchases, the choice of entity, and the way you pay yourself all affect how much a deduction is worth. Rewards are a nice bonus on top of that plan, not the plan itself.

## A simple way to choose

If you want a short checklist, start here:

- Total your annual card-eligible spending, excluding vendors who add surcharges.
- Find your top two categories and the months they peak.
- Compare a flat-rate card against a category card using your own numbers, including the annual fee.
- Confirm you can pay the full balance each month, even in your tightest month.
- Check that the card exports cleanly into your accounting software, so reconciliation stays quick.

The [SBA's guide to managing your business finances](https://www.sba.gov/business-guide/manage-your-business/manage-your-finances) is a useful companion if you are also reviewing credit, budgeting, and cash-flow practices more broadly.

## Common Questions

**Are credit card rewards taxable for a winery?**

Usually not. Cash back and points earned from purchases are generally treated as a rebate, not income. Sign-up bonuses that require no spending, and referral payments, can be taxable. Keep the card statements and any 1099s, and tell us how you record rewards so your books stay consistent.

**What is the best business credit card for a winery?**

The one that matches your spending. If bottling supplies, shipping, and advertising make up most of your spend, a card with bonus categories in those areas may win. If your spending is scattered, a flat 2 percent card with no annual fee is simpler and easier to reconcile.

**Should I pay my grape growers by credit card?**

Only if the grower does not add a surcharge and your rewards exceed any fee. A 3 percent surcharge against a 2 percent reward loses money. Many growers prefer checks or ACH, and those methods keep your credit limit free for harvest costs.
